extracted.subtask_description: Practical classroom assessment techniques for undergraduate mathematics courses, including written-homework guidelines, short in-class instruments, group-project evaluation, and assignments that connect mathematics to students' fields and careers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidelines for Written Homework (expository paragraph required)
rubrics_metrics.description: Your papers can be as expository as you want to make them. Tell how you arrived at your particular solution. You can discuss how the problem relates to material in class and possible applications of the problem. Do you understand the class material better now by working on this problem? Explain. If you could not arrive at a solution tell what you tried and why it didn’t work, or describe what you think may work. Vent frustrations! Identify obstacles you encountered and what you think you need to overcome these. The most important thing is to demonstrate to me that some thought went into your work and that you learned something! An expository paragraph describing their experience with the problem must be included with the solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a required expository paragraph with each homework solution that explains process, connections, and learning. Encourage students to describe failed attempts and obstacles. Use example prompts and model answers to show expectations. Initially penalize very shallow expository responses and omit-credit cases (deduct a few points for shallow sections; several points for missing the section) until students learn the conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess process as well as results (grade solution + exposition together)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the solution together with the exposition, giving one score for the combination. Reward process, not just results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give credit for thoughtful exposition even when solutions are incorrect if the student demonstrates understanding or reflection. Deduct points when expository sections are shallow or absent. Use students' paragraphs to decide class follow-ups and to create new problems; emphasize that the purpose is to show substantial thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggested prompts for expository sections
rubrics_metrics.description: Example questions to ask students in their expository writing: Do you understand more or less about this topic after this problem? Explain how you arrived at your solution. Discuss trials that didn’t work. Discuss possible alternate solutions. Discuss possible applications of this problem. Discuss the connections between this problem and our work on ____ in class. Describe what you were thinking and feeling while working on this problem. Can you think of a better problem to assign on this topic? If so, what is it?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide specific prompts early in the term to scaffold student responses; encourage additional comments beyond the prompts. As students gain confidence, allow more freedom. Use these prompts when expository responses are initially poor and require reworkings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design open-ended conjecture problems (value of conjecturing without proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use open-ended problems that ask students to make conjectures (not necessarily prove them) and to convince themselves that their guess is accurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open-ended/conjecture problems often produce richer expository comments and evidence of learning even if solutions are incorrect. These assignments are especially effective for prompting reflection and revealing student thinking processes; include explicit instructions that proof may not be required but reflection is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group Projects Evaluation Form (short instrument)
rubrics_metrics.description: A brief evaluation form for group projects: 1) Overall, how effectively did your groups work together on the project? (Poorly, Adequately, Well, Extremely Well). 2) In an effective working group, each person should be an active participant. How well did your groups meet this goal? (Poorly, Adequately, Well, Extremely Well). 3) Give one specific example of something you learned from a group that you probably would not have learned alone. 4) Give one specific example of something another group member learned from you that he or she probably would not have learned alone. 5) What is the biggest challenge to group projects? How could this challenge be overcome?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a short standardized form immediately after a project; tabulate responses quickly and return results to the class with a short summary and planned changes. Use item 3–4 to surface concrete learning gains; use item 5 to identify obstacles (e.g., scheduling) and propose remedies (e.g., using class time for group planning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting Course Goals activity
rubrics_metrics.description: At course start, present program goals and ask students to select which goals they believe are important to all graduates and to choose one which the course will help them achieve; then write a paragraph identifying the goal and why it is important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tabulate and share responses the next day to focus class on course mission and to solicit expectations. Revisit student-selected goals during the term when relevant examples arise. This creates buy-in and helps align instructor and student expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quick classroom assessment constraint (10-minute CATs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Favor assessment tools that use no more than ten minutes of class time and require no more than an hour after class to tabulate and form a response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quick instruments are more likely to be used repeatedly. However, plan ahead: identify what you want to learn, what you expect to find, and what you intend to do with the results; allocate time to evaluate and respond to student feedback, or the activity loses assessment value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mid-term adjustments (anonymous three-question feedback)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask students anonymously: 1) What’s one specific way that this class has addressed a goal? (what worked?) 2) What’s something that shouldn’t have happened? (what didn’t work?) 3) What’s something missing or unnoticed that should happen? (what’s missing so far?)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize results and report back to the class with intended actions (examples: arrange field trips, change use of videos, solicit volunteers). Use this focused instrument to react mid-term rather than waiting until course end; do not use as the first assessment tool—students must trust you will act on feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-Test Survey and Revising Goals (exam follow-up folder)
rubrics_metrics.description: After exams, have students resubmit tests with corrections, complete a Post-Test Survey (sample questions below), and revise their initial goals to produce five new ones based on class experience. Sample Post-Test Survey questions: (1) How prepared did you feel for this test? (2) Did you do as well as you expected? (3) Was the test fair? (4) On what questions did you make your mistakes and why? What did you feel were your weak areas? Be explicit. (5) How many hours per day do you actually study?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the folders to prompt self-assessment and to provide personalized feedback. Collate selected survey responses and display anonymously to prompt class discussion (e.g., fairness, study patterns). Use these materials to coach students and to refine future instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Library real-world translation assignment (getting into the real world)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignment: photocopy a page from an advanced text or journal in the student's chosen field that includes some calculus; document the source; write a one-page explanation of what the mathematics is saying in language understandable to another student in the class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grade primarily on effort; show model good/poor student work to set expectations. Because detailed mathematical feedback is time-consuming, use a form-letter approach with personalized comments appended. Use collected xeroxes on overhead to show applicability and ubiquity of calculus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resume/self-introduction assignment (looking good on a resume)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignment: write a two-page self-introduction to a potential employer presenting academic activities (including mathematics classes) as evidence of potential as an employee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use class time to discuss resume-building activities (clubs, research, tutoring, conferences). Collect these documents as artifacts; exceptional student work may be appended to recommendation letters. Demonstrate examples (former students' material, anonymized) to help students present themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use student expository writing to inform instruction and create new problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Use students' expository paragraphs to learn how they approach problems and to construct new problems, prepare lessons, and instigate classroom discussions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After reading paragraphs, design follow-up problems or class activities that respond to revealed misconceptions or insights (e.g., create a quadratic-over-Zn problem after students raise related questions). Use student comments to focus class review after grading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Success factors for expository writing assignments
rubrics_metrics.description: Expository writing works best for open-ended problems and not for routine symbol-manipulating problems; early assignments may yield trivial responses; requiring specific questions and showing peer work helps improve quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request reworkings when responses are trivial. Show transparencies or selected student outputs to provide feedback and model good work. Keep these assignments as a small portion of the grade but give timely feedback so students see their work matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group-work follow-up: return tabulated responses and a plan
rubrics_metrics.description: Return tabulated group evaluation responses promptly with a brief instructor paragraph summarizing what the instructor will do (e.g., devote class time to group discussion, schedule check-ins).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate, explicit instructor response reinforces the value of the evaluation and increases student buy-in. Use percentages and examples from responses to justify pedagogical adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t ask if you don’t want to know (assessment intent and follow-through)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before you solicit student responses, identify what you want to learn, what you think you will find, and what you intend to do with the results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you do not plan to act on feedback, the activity becomes a quiz or study tool rather than assessment. Make explicit to students how you will use responses and ensure you have time to evaluate and respond; that maintains the assessment quality of the activity.
